title: Exec Brief (Draft): Dedicated Tiers + Throughput SLO (Standard / Plus / Premium)
content:
Slide 1 — Title
Dedicated Tiers + Throughput SLO (Standard / Plus / Premium)
Exec review draft
Owner: Lauren Bishop (Product, Dedicated)
Reviewers: SRE (Sean), Infra/Fleet (Irene/Vanessa), Finance (Laura/Rishi), GTM (Soojin/Stephanie)

Speaker notes:
This is a packaging + reliability commitment update to make Dedicated purchases predictable and operationally supportable. Goal today: align on tier structure, customer-facing SLO language at a high level, and pricing bands/guardrails so we can finalize contract wording + rollout.


Slide 2 — Why this now
What’s changed:
- Dedicated demand is increasing and getting more enterprise-shaped (procurement requires written commitments)
- We currently sell “Dedicated” with inconsistent promises (tokens/sec, latency, “it depends”), causing escalations and custom one-offs
- GPU supply and regional heterogeneity are forcing standardized shapes + consistent capacity accounting
- We now have enough instrumentation to measure throughput reliably (post streaming accounting fix)

Customer pain we hear (recent calls):
- “What throughput is guaranteed, in writing, and how is it measured?” (AlphaBank / HyperDoc)
- “Can we burst? If yes, what happens to other tenants / our own floor?” (Vidorama)
- “If we miss, what’s the escalation path and remedy?” (Northstar Support)

Speaker notes:
This is a combined product + SRE + Finance effort. Without tiers we either over-promise (risk) or under-sell (lost deals). The tier model lets us manage headroom and give clearer commitments.


Slide 3 — Objectives + non-goals
Objectives:
- Define a throughput SLO for Dedicated that is measurable, enforceable, and hard to game
- Standardize tier entitlements (throughput floor, burst policy, failover posture, support response)
- Map tiers to standard hardware “shapes” by region with predictable perf profiles
- Provide pricing bands and discount guardrails to protect gross margin + reduce Deal Desk churn
- Operationalize with dashboards, alerts, runbooks, and CS escalation playbooks

Non-goals (v1):
- Not guaranteeing per-request latency (we will report it; no contractual latency SLO in v1)
- Not supporting arbitrary multi-model pinning with a single blended guarantee (requires follow-on)
- Not promising cross-region active/active for all tiers (Premium only; others best-effort failover)

Speaker notes:
We’re purposely keeping the v1 commitment focused: throughput floor for an agreed model/version + shape, measured at our edge. Latency remains an internal SLO + visible metric.


Slide 4 — Proposal at a glance
Three tiers:
- Standard: predictable baseline; best for steady workloads; lowest cost per committed unit
- Plus: higher floor + defined burst + faster support; optimized for growth-stage prod
- Premium: highest floor + stronger HA/failover posture + fastest response; for regulated/mission-critical

Core promise:
- Dedicated deployments get a throughput floor under defined conditions, measured continuously and reported.

Speaker notes:
We’re aligning product packaging to the operational reality: headroom, warm pools, and admission control differ by tier.


Slide 5 — Canonical metric: what we will measure
Metric (proposed canonical):
- “Effective output token throughput” at the deployment level, measured as output_tokens / second
- Aggregated over a rolling measurement window (see next slide)

Why output tokens:
- Stable across streaming/non-streaming after metric fix
- Maps to customer value (how fast they get completions)
- Less gameable than requests/sec across variable prompt sizes

Attribution:
- Per deployment_id, tagged by model_id + version + region + tier

Speaker notes:
ADR-027 captures why we chose deployment-level throughput vs per-route and why output tokens (not input+output). We will still expose both in dashboards; only one is contractual.


Slide 6 — Throughput SLO: proposed customer-facing language (draft)
Draft wording (for Order Form / SLO exhibit):
- “For the Dedicated Deployment and Model Version specified in the Order Form, Redwood will provide a monthly Throughput Service Level Objective (SLO) of at least [X] output tokens per second, measured as the 5-minute rolling average of Successful Output Tokens per second at Redwood’s service edge, during Eligible Time.”

Eligible Time (high-level):
- Excludes customer-induced throttling / backpressure (e.g., client disconnects, cancelled streams)
- Excludes scheduled maintenance windows with notice (per MSA)
- Applies only when requests meet documented input constraints (max context, max output, supported parameters)
- Applies only to the pinned model version / agreed compatibility set

Remedy (high-level direction):
- Service credits tied to SLO miss severity and duration (Finance/Legal final language pending)

Speaker notes:
The intent is to be explicit and auditable: how measured, where measured, and what doesn’t count. Legal will translate to contract-grade language; this slide is the product/SRE intent.


Slide 7 — Measurement details (v1)
Window + statistics:
- Primary: 5-minute rolling average evaluated continuously
- Reporting: monthly compliance summary + incident annotations

Inclusions:
- Successful responses (HTTP 2xx) and streamed tokens delivered to the client

Exclusions / edge cases:
- Retries after client timeouts not double-counted (post PR-19422)
- Tokens generated after client disconnect are excluded
- Customer concurrency above documented client guidance may increase queueing; if admission control sheds requests, shed requests do not count toward throughput numerator

Speaker notes:
We want to avoid “SLO by denial”: shedding to preserve throughput can’t make the metric look better; numerator only counts delivered tokens. We’ll separately monitor rejected requests as a saturation signal.


Slide 8 — Tier entitlements (summary)
Standard
- Throughput floor: defined per shape + model class
- Burst: best-effort within the same pool (no reserved burst)
- Failover: best-effort within region; no cross-region guarantee
- Support: standard enterprise response targets

Plus
- Higher throughput floor (more headroom)
- Burst: defined burst allowance into a shared burst pool (metered)
- Failover: best-effort within region + prioritized recovery
- Support: faster response + proactive comms during incidents

Premium
- Highest floor + stricter admission control protections
- Burst: defined burst allowance + optional reserved burst add-on (region dependent)
- Failover: stronger posture (warm spares / HA depending on region/shape); cross-region failover option for eligible models
- Support: fastest response, named escalation path

Speaker notes:
Exact numbers are set in pricing/packaging doc and depend on region/shape. The key is that entitlements map directly to operational knobs: headroom, warm pools, and paging policy.


Slide 9 — Shapes: standardization to make commitments real
Why shapes:
- Throughput depends heavily on GPU type, count, interconnect, and CPU/RAM/network constraints
- Standard shapes reduce variance, simplify provisioning, and make SLOs enforceable

Shape catalog approach:
- Per region: small set of supported shapes (e.g., L40S-based, A100-based, H100-based)
- Each shape has:
  - Supported model families + context/output limits
  - Baseline throughput bands per model class (benchmarked)
  - Recommended max concurrency + batching configuration

Speaker notes:
Infra will not commit to bespoke “kitchen sink” clusters. If a customer wants a non-standard shape, it becomes a custom SKU outside of tier commitments (or Premium exception with explicit carve-outs).


Slide 10 — Pricing: proposed bands + guardrails (v1)
Packaging principles:
- Price on committed throughput units (anchored to shape) + tier multiplier for entitlements
- Keep list prices simple enough for quoting; complexity stays in the shape catalog + sizing guidance
- Protect GM by enforcing headroom assumptions and limiting discounting where supply is tight

Pricing bands (exec-level view, not final list):
- Standard: lowest $/committed token/sec; minimal reserved headroom
- Plus: mid-band; priced to include burst reserve + higher support cost allocation
- Premium: highest; priced to include HA posture (warm spares) + strictest headroom targets

Discount guardrails (direction):
- Standard: moderate discounting allowed at volume
- Plus: tighter; Deal Desk approval above threshold
- Premium: tightest; exceptions require Finance sign-off + supply confirmation by Fleet

Speaker notes:
Finance has the detailed unit economics model. Today we’re asking for alignment on pricing structure and guardrails; exact list will be in the v1 pricing doc and quote tooling.


Slide 11 — What changes operationally
Enforcement + protection:
- Tier-aware admission control to preserve floors under saturation (ENG-19257)
- Tier→pool/shape routing with safe defaults + feature flag rollout (ENG-19263)
- Metering for burst usage vs committed usage (ENG-19302)

Visibility:
- Per-customer dashboard showing committed floor, actual throughput, saturation signals
- Burn-rate alerting + paging policy tied to tier (ENG-19288)

Support/CS:
- Standard escalation playbook for SLO misses and customer comms
- Credit hooks tied to validated SLO breach

Speaker notes:
This is not “a slideware SLA.” We’re aligning routing, capacity, and billing with the commitment. Without admission control + metering, we can’t safely promise burst.


Slide 12 — Key risks + mitigations
Risk: GPU supply constraints by region (especially premium shapes)
- Mitigation: limited shape catalog; publish lead times; Premium availability by region; warm spare requirements only where supply supports it

Risk: Measurement disputes (“your dashboard says X, ours says Y”)
- Mitigation: contract defines measurement point (Redwood edge), publish metric definitions + examples, keep a customer-visible view consistent with internal

Risk: Model variability + customer prompt distribution shifts can cause perf drift
- Mitigation: commit to model version + documented parameter/input constraints; require re-benchmark on major model upgrades; publish “supported workload envelopes”

Risk: SLO can be gamed via tiny outputs or cancellation patterns
- Mitigation: exclude cancelled/disconnected streams; define eligible requests; monitor abuse patterns; keep separate “attempted vs delivered” metrics

Risk: Alert noise / operational burden during early rollout
- Mitigation: tune burn-rate thresholds in beta; gate Premium promises until dashboards/alerts are stable; oncall playbooks

Speaker notes:
The biggest failure mode is promising more than the fleet can deliver in constrained regions. Second is unclear measurement. Both are addressed with standard shapes + explicit measurement language.


Slide 13 — Rollout plan
Phase 0 (now): internal alignment + docs
- Finalize PRD + SLO doc + ADR
- Pricing v1: bands, list, guardrails

Phase 1: limited GA (beta cohort)
- Target: ~5–10 existing Dedicated customers who have asked for commitments (mix of Plus/Premium)
- Runbook-driven provisioning, benchmark validation, dashboard review with customer
- Weekly retro on metric stability + incident response

Phase 2: broader availability
- Enablement: seller cheat sheet, quoting workflow, Console tier/SLO widget
- Default all new Dedicated deals to tiered SKUs; reduce bespoke exceptions

Phase 3: contract standardization
- Update Order Form templates and MSA exhibit language
- Add compliance reporting cadence and credit workflow

Speaker notes:
We should treat the first cohort as a product launch with tight feedback loops. If we can’t clearly show the floor and how we computed it, we’re not ready for enterprise procurement.


Slide 14 — Decision asks (exec)
We need decisions/approval on:
1) Tiering structure (Standard / Plus / Premium) and entitlement direction
2) The throughput SLO measurement point + window (deployment-level, 5-min rolling avg; monthly compliance)
3) Shape standardization principle (limited supported shapes per region; exceptions are explicitly non-standard)
4) Pricing structure (commit on throughput units anchored to shape; tier multipliers) + discount guardrails direction
5) Rollout approach (limited GA cohort before broad enablement)

Open items to resolve post-approval:
- Final legal language and credit schedule
- Exact throughput floors per tier/shape/model class (benchmarked)
- Regional availability matrix + lead-time policy

Speaker notes:
If we agree on these five, the team can finalize docs/tooling and start the limited GA.


Slide 15 — Appendix: FAQ (draft)
Q: Is this a latency guarantee?
- A: Not in v1 contract language. Latency is reported and monitored; throughput floor is the formal commitment.

Q: What about multiple models in one deployment?
- A: v1: SLO applies to the specified model/version. Multi-model requires either separate deployments or explicit carve-out.

Q: Can customers exceed the throughput floor?
- A: Yes. Floor is guaranteed under eligible conditions; actual throughput may be higher. Burst is tier-dependent and may be metered.

Q: How do we handle model upgrades?
- A: New model version = new perf envelope. Upgrade requires validation; the commitment attaches to the pinned version.

Q: What do we do when we miss?
- A: Follow escalation playbook: validate metric, triage capacity/saturation, communicate ETA, and apply credits per policy if breach is confirmed.

Speaker notes:
These are the questions Sales/CS are already getting. We should keep answers consistent and avoid ad-hoc commitments.
